title: Author's word choices
keyIdea: Authors pick each word on purpose. One verb can change how a thing moves, a few words can turn a scene from cosy to spooky, kind or unkind words decide how you feel about a character, and short or long sentences change how fast a story feels. Good readers ask: why this word, and what does it make me see or feel?

kid: An author picks every word on purpose. The dog walked. The dog raced. The dog crept. Each word makes a new picture in your head.
Words can set a mood. A dark night where the wind howled feels spooky. A sunny day where birds sang feels safe. Only a few words changed.
Words can make you like someone, or not. Sam is curious sounds nice. Sam is nosy sounds rude. They mean much the same, but they feel different.
Short bits make a story feel fast. Run. Now. Go! Long, smooth sentences feel slow and calm. Ask: why did the author pick this word?
adult: From about seven to nine, children start to notice that authors make choices on purpose. They also see that those choices change how a reader feels. The main tools at this age are strong verbs, such as crept instead of went, and mood words, such as gloomy or bright. Others are the feel of a word, such as curious or nosy, and sentence length, which sets the pace.

The lab gives each idea its own action. Children swap one verb and watch a dog move. They pick three words that turn a sunny night spooky. They choose the kinder of two words for the same girl. They decide which of two versions feels faster or calmer. Then they explain why an author chose a word such as howled.

Watch for three common mistakes. One is thinking any word with the same meaning will do, so nosy and curious seem the same. Another is thinking short sentences are always better, when long smooth ones suit calm scenes. The third is answering why by just repeating the word. A good answer names the effect: it makes the wind sound like a wild animal.
To help at home, stop on a strong word while you read together. Ask: what does this word make you see? How would it change with a plain word instead?

familyTip: While reading together, swap a strong word for a plain one (crept becomes went) and ask: which picture is better, and why do you think the author chose that word?

visual.caption: Does each word make the scene feel cosy or spooky? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: swap a verb, turn a sunny night spooky, pick kind or unkind words for Sam, match sentence length to pace, and say why a word was chosen.

practice.prompt: Which word shows the mouse moved very quietly?
practice.hint: Think of a word for moving softly so no one hears you.
practice.explain: Crept means moved slowly and quietly. Went is plain, and stamped is loud.

practice.prompt: A story has {n} short sentences in a row: Bang. Run. Hide. How does it feel?
practice.hint: Read short bits out loud. Do they feel quick or slow?
practice.explain: Short sentences, like these {n}, are quick to read, so the story feels fast and tense.

practice.prompt: Which word makes you like Jo more?
practice.hint: All three mean Jo will not give up. Which one sounds like a good thing?
practice.explain: Determined sounds like a strength. Stubborn and pig-headed say the same thing in an unkind way.

practice.prompt: "The thunder growled for {n} minutes." Why did the author pick growled?
choices: It makes the thunder sound like an angry animal.
It tells you the thunder was quiet.
practice.hint: What kind of thing usually growls? How does that make the thunder feel?
practice.explain: Dogs and bears growl when they are angry, so for all {n} minutes the thunder sounds fierce and alive.

pool.prompt: Which sentence makes the house feel spooky?
choices: The old house creaked in the dark.
The bright house was full of laughter.
pool.hint: Look for words about sounds and light that feel creepy.
pool.explain: Creaked and dark make you feel uneasy. Big is plain, and bright and laughter feel happy.

pool.prompt: "Tom gobbled his {n} chips." What does gobbled show?
pool.hint: Say gobbled out loud. Is it a slow word or a fast word?
pool.explain: Gobbled means ate quickly and greedily, so all {n} chips went fast.

pool.prompt: "Ava is slim" and "Ava is skinny." What is different?
pool.hint: They mean nearly the same, but how do they feel?
pool.explain: Both say Ava is thin, but slim sounds nice and skinny can sound rude. The feeling is different.

pool.prompt: An author wants a calm bedtime scene. Which fits best?
choices: The stars came out one by one as the sleepy town grew quiet.
pool.hint: Calm scenes use slow, smooth sentences and gentle words.
pool.explain: The long, gentle sentence feels slow and calm. The short bits and the crash feel fast and jumpy.

pool.prompt: A child says the author chose stomped because "it says stomped". What is missing?
choices: The effect: it shows the person was cross
Nothing, that is a full answer
The number of letters in the word
pool.hint: A why answer should say what the word makes you see or feel.
pool.explain: Saying the word again does not explain it. Stomped shows heavy, loud steps, so the person seems cross.

pool.prompt: In a race, the runner {n} times faster than the rest. Which verb fits the gap best?
pool.hint: Pick the word that sounds fastest.
pool.explain: Zoomed shows great speed, so it fits a runner {n} times faster. Wandered and shuffled are slow words.

pool.prompt: Which word makes the sea sound gentle?
choices: The sea whispered on the sand.
The sea roared on the rocks.
pool.hint: A whisper is soft. A roar is loud.
pool.explain: Whispered makes the sea sound soft and gentle. Roared and smashed make it sound wild and strong.
